q: To overthrow his former opinions, Descartes says he doesn't need to prove each one false. Instead he will:
a: Attack the foundations of his opinions
w: Examine every one of his beliefs one by one
Accept only beliefs approved by the Church
Keep only beliefs that most people share
e: Reject any opinion in which he finds any occasion for doubt, by attacking their foundations. Once the foundation (the senses) is undermined, everything built on it falls 'of its own accord'.

q: What is the main source Descartes says all his previously accepted 'truths' came from?
w: Scripture
Mathematics
Teachers and books
e: 'Whatever I have hitherto admitted as most true, that I received either from, or by my Senses', and the senses sometimes deceive.

q: Descartes' response to 'surely I can't doubt I'm sitting by the fire in my winter gown' is:
a: He has often dreamed exactly such things
w: Only madmen would doubt such obvious things
God guarantees that his senses are reliable
He might be a brain in a vat in a lab
e: He has often dreamed exactly such things while lying in bed. The dreaming argument: there are no sure signs to distinguish waking from sleep.

q: Descartes uses the analogy of painters inventing mermaids and satyrs to argue that even dream images are built from:
a: Simpler, more universal things like shape and number
w: Divine ideas that God has planted in our minds
Memories of real creatures seen in distant lands
Nothing at all, since dreams are made from nothing
e: Simpler, more universal things (extension, shape, quantity, number, place, time). Even a wholly invented picture uses real colors. Likewise dreams are composed of simple, general things.

q: After the dreaming argument, which sciences does Descartes initially think still contain something certain?
w: Physics and medicine
Astronomy
Biology
e: 'Whether I sleep or wake, two and three added make five.' Sciences of composite things (physics, astronomy, medicine) are doubtful.

q: What possibility makes Descartes doubt even that 2 + 3 = 5?
a: An all-powerful deceiver who makes him err
w: The possibility that he is dreaming right now
His teachers may have lied to him as a child
Numbers might not exist in the physical world
e: An omnipotent God (or deceiver) could make him err whenever he adds. The dreaming argument leaves math intact. The deceiver hypothesis extends doubt to math too.

q: Descartes compares his tendency to slip back into old opinions to:
a: A prisoner who dreams of liberty
w: A sailor lost at sea in a storm
A child slowly learning to walk
An architect building on sand
e: A prisoner who dreams of liberty and is afraid to wake. He willingly falls back into comfortable opinions, fearing the toilsome waking of doubt.

q: Descartes begins Meditation II feeling as though he has:
w: Climbed to the top of a mountain
Woken from a long, deep sleep
Been released from a dark prison
e: Fallen into a deep whirlpool/gulf where he can neither touch bottom nor swim to the top. Yesterday's doubts left him 'plunged on a sudden into a deep gulf'.

a: He needed just one firm point to move the Earth
w: He discovered displacement while in his bathtub
He proved the true value of pi with polygons
He doubted the existence of the external world
e: Needed only one firm, immovable point to move the whole Earth. Likewise, Descartes needs just one certain, indisputable truth.

q: In Meditation II, 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true:
a: Whenever it is spoken or thought by me
w: Only when I perceive my body
Only if God exists
At all times, whether or not I think
e: Even if the deceiver deceives me, I must exist to be deceived. The certainty holds 'whilst I think that I am'.

q: Which faculty does Descartes find cannot be separated from himself?
w: Nutrition
Locomotion
Bodily sensation
e: Thought (the cogitative faculty). Nutrition and motion need a body, and sensing happens in dreams too. 'Thought, this alone cannot be separated from me.'

q: Descartes concludes he is 'only a thinking thing'. Which of these does he include in thinking?
w: Only reasoning and mathematical calculation
Only the perception of external bodies
Digestion, breathing and bodily movement
e: Doubting, understanding, affirming, denying, willing, imagining, and sensing. A thinking thing doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, imagines and perceives.

q: Why does Descartes say he can't use imagination to learn what he is?
a: Imagining means picturing a body, and bodies are in doubt
w: Imagination is always accurate, so it proves nothing new
Imagination is a bodily organ that he cannot examine
He believes he has no faculty of imagination at all
e: To imagine is to contemplate the image of a corporeal thing, and bodies are still in doubt. Using imagination to know the self would be like falling asleep to see something more clearly in a dream.

q: In the wax example, after the wax is melted by the fire, what remains of the wax?
a: Only something extended, flexible and changeable
w: Its smell and color, though both are weaker
Its hardness and the sound it makes when struck
Nothing at all, since the wax has disappeared
e: Every sensory quality changed, yet it's the same wax. So what we know of it isn't given by the senses.

q: The wax example concludes that we know bodies through:
w: Sight and touch together
The faculty of imagination
Memory of past experience
e: The inspection of the mind (understanding) alone. Imagination can't run through the wax's innumerable possible changes. Only the understanding grasps what the wax is.

q: Descartes looks out the window and 'sees' men in the street, though he only sees hats and coats that could cover automata. The point is:
a: We judge with the mind what we think we see
w: People are really just complicated machines
Vision is perfectly reliable when we look closely
Clothing reveals a person's true essence
e: What we think we see with the eyes, we actually judge with the mind. He judges them to be men by his 'judicative faculty', not by sight alone.

q: What is the final conclusion of Meditation II?
a: Nothing is known more easily than his own mind
w: His body is better known to him than his mind
God exists and could never deceive him at all
The whole external world is only an illusion
e: Nothing can be perceived more easily or evidently than one's own mind. Every act of perceiving the wax gives even more evidence of the mind doing the perceiving.
